Use this page if your study needs to link a child to its parents, and from
there to siblings or to a parent's characteristics. It is the first step of a
[sibling design](special-designs.qmd#sibling-designs), and also of any study
that needs the mother's or father's education, income or diagnoses.

## What the link is {#what-the-link-is}

BEF has two columns for the link: `mor_id` and `far_id`, the person id of the
mother and of the father. They come from the Civil Registration System (CPR).
Three things about them are easy to miss.

**They are the legal parents, not necessarily the biological ones.** CPR holds
the legal relationship, and it keeps only the current one: "Danish legislation
prohibits the CRS of keeping information on previous legal relationships. Thus,
for example, for adopted children, the CRS contains information on the legal
parents only" (Pedersen et al. 2006). Statistics Denmark (DST) is more careful
still: "Parent child relations in CPR is an administrative relations, which
cannot necessarily be sided be legal or biological parent-child relations"
(DST, documentation of the *Relatives* statistics, accuracy and reliability).
The Medical Birth Register records a different relation: "parents in the MBR
are the (assumed) biological parents, whereas the parents registered in the
Danish Civil Registration System are the legal parents and thus not
necessarily equivalent to the former (unless a paternity trial has been
resolved)" (Bliddal et al. 2018). See [The mother at birth](#mfr).

**A missing id means no link is registered.** It does not mean the parent is
unknown to the family. See the coverage table below.

**A parent can be of the other sex than the column.** A co-mother is registered
in the father's place, and DST marks that in FTBARN (see [Adoption and other
non-biological relations](#adoption)).

## Coverage by birth cohort {#coverage}

BEF takes `mor_id` and `far_id` from CPR. The shares below are for persons born in
Denmark, from CPR as it stood in 2006 (Pedersen et al. 2006). They are the nearest guide to what your
delivery holds, but count the missing links in your own data.

  | Born in Denmark | Link to a mother | Link to a father |
  | --------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
  | 1950            | 8.0%             | 7.6%             |
  | 1960            | 98.7%            | 95.7%            |
  | 1970            | 99.9%            | 99.2%            |

The same paper says the links for persons born in Denmark in 1969 or later are
"considered to be 100% correct", and those for 1960-1968 "almost correct",
because the links for 1969-1978 were checked against the parish registers
(Pedersen et al. 2006).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why older cohorts have fewer links"}
CPR started in 1968, and the parental links were first built from families
living at the same address. Until 1978 a link was erased when the child moved
away from home, when a parent moved, when the child had children or when the
child turned 18. From 1978 links are kept permanently, and from then on they
follow the legal relationship (Pedersen et al. 2006).

You may also read that everyone born in Denmark in 1960 or later has a complete
link to both parents (Pedersen 2013). That is about the Family Relations
Database at the National Centre for Register-based Research (NCRR), which keeps
only the links it deems valid. It is not a description of `mor_id` and `far_id`
in BEF.
:::

For people **born abroad** the links are much rarer, because parent and child are
not linked at immigration, and a parent needs a Danish CPR number to be linked at
all (Pedersen et al. 2006; DST, *Relatives*, accuracy and reliability). In
Pedersen et al., 29.8% of those born abroad in 1980 and 94.2% of those born in
1990 have a mother link. Expect a missing `mor_id` and `far_id` for most
immigrants, and report the share.

For **newborns**, the second parent can be missing for up to half a year after
the birth, because it takes that long to register. DST names this as most
common for births in the second half of a year and for unmarried parents, and
advises against studying the relatives of newborns in the latest reference
year (DST, *Relatives*, accuracy and reliability).

Persons born before 1967 have too few registered parents and siblings, and for
those born before 1935 the undercount may be very large (DST, *Relatives*,
accuracy and reliability).

## Step 1 - Take the link from BEF {#step-1}

BEF is a snapshot register (see [DST pitfalls](dst-pitfalls.qmd), pitfall 5), so
the same child has one row per snapshot, and `mor_id` and `far_id` can differ
between snapshots or be missing in some of them. A parent can be added to the
child after the first snapshots, for example. There is no single correct value,
so you have to pick a rule and write it in your methods.

The rule below takes, for each child, the first non-missing value from the
snapshots at or after the child's birth. For a child born before the first BEF
snapshot (December 1985) that is the link as it stood in 1985 or later.

The rule is written as a function, because [Step 3](#siblings) runs it again
for the siblings outside your cohort.

```r
# Step 1: one mother and one father per child, from BEF ------------------------
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(dplyr)   # the verbs are translated to SQL and run in DuckDB

# pnrs: the children you want parents for. Returns one row per child with at
# least one registered parent: pnr | foed_dag | mor_id | far_id
parents_from_bef <- function(pnrs) {
  bef <- read_register("bef") %>%
    rename_with(tolower) %>%
    semi_join(tibble(pnr = pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
    # a missing id is an empty string, not NA, in parquet converted from SAS
    mutate(mor_id = na_if(mor_id, ""), far_id = na_if(far_id, ""))
  # Columns: pnr | foed_dag | mor_id | far_id | referencetid

  # The first non-missing mother id in a snapshot at or after birth
  mother <- bef %>%
    filter(referencetid >= foed_dag, !is.na(mor_id)) %>%
    group_by(pnr) %>%
    slice_min(referencetid, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(pnr, foed_dag, mor_id)

  father <- bef %>%
    filter(referencetid >= foed_dag, !is.na(far_id)) %>%
    group_by(pnr) %>%
    slice_min(referencetid, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(pnr, foed_dag_far = foed_dag, far_id)

  # full_join on pnr: a child with only one registered parent keeps its row,
  # with NA for the other. BEF can correct a birth date between snapshots, so
  # foed_dag is taken from the mother's snapshot, or the father's if she is
  # missing, rather than used as a key.
  mother %>%
    full_join(father, by = "pnr") %>%
    mutate(foed_dag = coalesce(foed_dag, foed_dag_far)) %>%
    select(pnr, foed_dag, mor_id, far_id) %>%
    collect()
}

# cohort_pnrs: the pnr of the people in your cohort
parents <- parents_from_bef(cohort_pnrs)
```

A child with no link in BEF to either parent is not in `parents` at all. Join
`parents` back onto your cohort with `left_join()`, count the children with
`NA` for both by birth year before you go on, and report how many children each
analysis loses on that account.

Two things to check in your own delivery. A missing id in parquet converted
from SAS is an empty string, not `NA`, because a SAS text column has no missing
value of its own; the `na_if()` line turns it into `NA`, and without it every
child without a registered father would share the father id `""`. And if your
BEF has no `referencetid` column, order the snapshots by the `year` column the
parquet conversion adds: drop `referencetid >= foed_dag` from the two filters
and write `slice_min(year, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)`. A child is in BEF only
from birth, so this takes the first year with an id. If your delivery has
several snapshots a year, keep one per year first, as under "Check your BEF" in
[Socioeconomic variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#faik-income). A
different rule, such as the most frequent value or the latest snapshot, is
equally valid if you state it. What matters is that the rule is the same for
every child.

### The mother at birth: the Medical Birth Register {#mfr}

BEF holds the parents CPR has now. The Medical Birth Register (MFR) holds, for
each birth in Denmark, the (assumed) biological parents (Bliddal et al. 2018).
Sundhedsdatastyrelsen takes the link between mother and child from CPR
("udtræk fra CPR som giver den fornødne kobling mellem mor og barn", [register
declaration](https://cdn1.gopublic.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/Media/638650989716795161/Registerdeklaration%20for%20foedselsregisteret.pdf),
section 0.7), and Bliddal et al. describe the identification of the mother for
linkage as "virtually complete and ... of very high validity".

MFR is the better source of the mother when:

- the child may have been adopted, because BEF then holds the adoptive parents;
- the child was stillborn or died soon after birth. MFR has every birth, live
  or stillborn (register declaration, section 1.1), and a child who died
  before the next BEF snapshot is in no snapshot at all;
- you need twins and other multiple births, which MFR records
  (`barnsnummer_flerfoldsfoedsel`).

DST has no MFR table for births from 1973 to 1996. For those years FTBARN's
`mor1`, the first mother registered in CPR, is the nearest equivalent (see
[Adoption](#adoption)).

Two limits:

- **Births in Denmark only, and until 2018 only to mothers with a Danish CPR
  number** (register declaration, section 1.2). From 2019 a birth counts even
  if the mother has no Danish CPR number, so check `ErCPRnummerGyldigt_Mor`
  before you join on the mother's number.
- **The declaration says where the mother's link comes from, not the
  father's.** Compare `cpr_fader` with `far_id` in BEF before you rely on it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="MFR's column names, and a check of BEF against MFR"}
| Births         | Table          | Child            | Mother           | Father           |
| -------------- | -------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| 1997-2018      | `mfr`          | `cpr_barn`       | `cpr_moder`      | `cpr_fader`      |
| 2019 and later | `mfr_nyfoedte` | `CPRnummer_Barn` | `CPRnummer_Mor`  | `CPRnummer_Far`  |

```r
# The parents at birth from MFR (births 1997-2018), beside BEF's -------------
mfr_parents <- read_register("mfr") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  select(pnr = cpr_barn, mor_mfr = cpr_moder, far_mfr = cpr_fader) %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
  collect()

# How often is BEF's mother not the mother at birth?
parents %>%
  inner_join(mfr_parents, by = "pnr") %>%
  count(same_mother = mor_id == mor_mfr)
```
:::

## Step 2 - Check for adoption with FTBARN {#adoption}

Do this before you build siblings. BEF only has the current legal parents, so
an adopted child shares `mor_id` and `far_id` with its adoptive parents' other
children, and Step 3 would make them siblings. BEF cannot tell you whether the
relation is adoptive. FTBARN, the child file of the fertility database, can.
It has one row per child from 1973 and, besides the parents (`mor1`, `far1`),
two columns that mark the relation: `mor_foed_adop` for the mother and
`far_foed_adop` for the father.

DST describes them as marking whether information in the background registers
(the Adoption Register, CPR and the Medical Birth Register) points to an
adoptive or other non-biological relation. Codes 11 to 18 are a presumed
non-biological relation, codes 21 to 23 a presumed biological one, and 30 to 39
cover children born abroad, children born before 1973 and relations with no
sign of adoption or early registration. For the father the year in that last
group is 1991, not 1973: DST's grouping for `far_foed_adop` puts children born
before 1991 in 30 to 39 ([DST,
FAR_FOED_ADOP](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/Times/fertilitetsdatabasen/far-foed-adop)).
Codes 21 to 23 therefore mark a presumed biological father only for children
born from 1991. In the code below the father of an earlier child is "unknown"
even when nothing suggests an adoption, so excluding children with an
"unknown" father would drop almost every child born before 1991. The full list
is in the [value sets under FTBARN](register-reference.qmd#ftbarn).

Four points from DST's own documentation:

- **It is presumed, not known.** DST: "A biological relation can only be
  determined with a DNA test, which is not available in the background
  registers" (our translation). A child conceived with donor sperm or donor egg
  looks like a biological relation in the registers.
- **Do not count adoptions with it.** DST: "It makes no sense to count the
  number of adopted or biological relations from the variable" (our
  translation). Use it to select or exclude, not to estimate how many.
- **Code 14 is not an adoption.** It marks a parent of the other sex than the
  column, so a co-mother is registered in the father's column with code 14.
- **Code 12 can concern the other parent.** The child is in the Adoption
  Register, but the adoptive relation may be to the other parent.

In FTBARN, `mor1` is the first mother valid in CPR, and `mor2` the latest one
when it differs. The relation of `mor1` to the child is in `mor_foed_adop`.

::: {.callout-warning title="No adoption markers for 2019-2023, and wrong ones in older deliveries"}
DST changed the adoption columns in a correction of 30 October 2025. Version 2
of the fertility tables for reference years up to 2023 sets
`mor_foed_adop` and `far_foed_adop` to unknown (99) for 2019 to 2023, because
data are missing to form new adoption markers for those years. Version 1 held
other values by mistake. For children born in 2019 to 2023 adoption therefore
cannot be identified in FTBARN, and a delivery made before the correction has
wrong values for those years (DST, FTBARN register history). Check the `version`
column in your delivery.
:::

The code below sorts each parent into DST's groups. Codes 31 to 39, 99 and a
missing value all become "unknown": a child in those groups is not
non-biological, it is a child the registers cannot say anything about.

```r
# Step 2: adoption markers for the cohort (FTBARN) ------------------------------
ftbarn <- read_register("ftbarn") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
  select(pnr, mor1, far1, mor_foed_adop, far_foed_adop) %>%
  collect()

# DST's groups for the codes in mor_foed_adop and far_foed_adop
foed_adop_group <- function(code) {
  code <- as.integer(code)
  case_when(
    code %in% 21:23 ~ "presumed biological",
    code %in% 11:18 ~ "presumed non-biological",
    code == 0       ~ "no parent",
    .default        = "unknown"   # 31-39, 99 (2019-2023) and missing;
                                  # for fathers, nearly every child born before 1991
  )
}

ftbarn <- ftbarn %>%
  mutate(
    mother_relation = foed_adop_group(mor_foed_adop),
    father_relation = foed_adop_group(far_foed_adop)
  )
```

State in your methods that the group is *presumed* biological, and how many
children were "unknown". If your cohort has children born before 1991, their
fathers are "unknown" because of DST's rule, not because of an adoption, so say
how you treat them.

## Step 3 - Siblings {#siblings}

Siblings are children with the same parent id, and the type depends on how many
parents they share:

- **Full siblings** share both mother and father.
- **Maternal half-siblings** share the mother only, and **paternal
  half-siblings** share the father only.

Do not count a pair as full siblings when one of the fathers is missing. The
pair shares a mother, so it is at least a maternal half-sibling pair, and the
father is unknown. The code below gives those pairs their own type ("maternal,
father unknown"). Say in your methods how you handle them, and run the
analysis both ways if there are many of them.

The siblings you need are not only the ones in your cohort. If the exposed
child has a brother who is not in the cohort, he is still a sibling. So first
find everyone in BEF who has the same mother or father as someone in your
cohort, and run the rule from Step 1 for them too.

If your design needs biological siblings, use the groups from Step 2 to decide
which children to keep, for example only children whose mother and father are
both "presumed biological", and say so in your methods.

```r
# Step 3: sibling pairs and their type ----------------------------------------

# 3a: everyone who has the same mother or father as someone in the cohort
parent_ids <- tibble(id = unique(c(na.omit(parents$mor_id), na.omit(parents$far_id))))
bef_all    <- read_register("bef") %>% rename_with(tolower)
family_pnrs <- union(
  bef_all %>% semi_join(parent_ids, by = c("mor_id" = "id"), copy = TRUE) %>% distinct(pnr),
  bef_all %>% semi_join(parent_ids, by = c("far_id" = "id"), copy = TRUE) %>% distinct(pnr)
) %>%
  collect() %>%
  pull(pnr)

# 3b: the same rule as in Step 1, for the cohort and their siblings
family <- parents_from_bef(union(cohort_pnrs, family_pnrs))

# 3c: pairs of children with the same id in `key` (mor_id or far_id)
pairs_by <- function(key) {
  a <- family %>% rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_a"))
  b <- family %>% rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_b"))
  by <- setNames(paste0(key, "_b"), paste0(key, "_a"))
  a %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[paste0(key, "_a")]])) %>%
    # keep = TRUE: both id columns stay. many-to-many: a mother with three
    # children matches each child three times, which is what we want here.
    inner_join(b, by = by, keep = TRUE, relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
    filter(pnr_a < pnr_b)
}

# 3d: the type of each pair. A pair found through both parents appears twice,
# with the same type, and distinct() keeps one.
sibling_pairs <- bind_rows(pairs_by("mor_id"), pairs_by("far_id")) %>%
  mutate(
    same_mother = coalesce(mor_id_a == mor_id_b, FALSE),
    same_father = coalesce(far_id_a == far_id_b, FALSE),
    father_unknown = is.na(far_id_a) | is.na(far_id_b),
    mother_unknown = is.na(mor_id_a) | is.na(mor_id_b),
    type = case_when(
      same_mother & same_father    ~ "full",
      same_mother & father_unknown ~ "maternal, father unknown",
      same_father & mother_unknown ~ "paternal, mother unknown",
      same_mother                  ~ "maternal half",
      same_father                  ~ "paternal half"
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct(pnr_a, pnr_b, type)
```

The `famnet` package by Luke Johnston finds sibling pairs with
`fmn_siblings()`, labelling each pair "sibling" without the split into full
and half siblings above. It is on GitHub only, so it may not install on your
project. See [Algorithms and packages](packages-overview.qmd).

For a sibling analysis you also need a family id for the strata. For full siblings the
mother and father ids together identify the family. With half-siblings in the data, a person can belong to
more than one family, so decide how the strata are formed and state it.

## Step 4 - A parent's characteristic at the child's birth {#parent-characteristics}

Use `mor_id` or `far_id` as the `pnr` of the parent, and look the parent up in
the register that holds the characteristic, in the year that matters. That
could be the mother's education, income or employment at the child's birth, or
her diagnoses before it. The year rule is the one for any other person, so it
is not repeated here. See [When each dimension is
measured](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#timing) for education, employment and
income.

Before you do this, check that the parent ids match the person ids in the
registers you look them up in. Most non-missing `mor_id` values should appear
as a `pnr` in BEF. If they do not, the ids are not comparable in your project
and the lookup will return nothing.

A parent who was not living in Denmark in the year, or who died before it,
will have no row. That is a missing value in your analysis, so handle it as one
(see [Missing data](missing-data.qmd)).

## What to write in your methods {#methods}

- The source of the link (BEF `mor_id` and `far_id`, MFR for the parents at
  birth, FTBARN if you use it) and the rule for choosing between snapshots.
- That the link is the legal, administrative relation in CPR.
- The birth cohorts you include and the share with a missing parent link, by
  birth year, and how immigrants were handled.
- How half-siblings and pairs with a missing parent were handled.
- If you use the adoption markers, which codes you used and that the relation
  is presumed.
